sentences.text: Mandasuchus was a four-legged meat-eater with a notably long neck.
Although several well-preserved skeletons exist, very few skull parts have been found.
The only known tooth is thin and features serrated edges.
Its longest neck vertebrae have centers that are roughly 1.8 times longer than they are tall.
Two staggered rows of bony plates ran along its back to form uneven armor.
The ankle joint worked like a modern crocodile's, with a peg fitting into a pit.
Alan Charig first mentioned the genus in 1956, but it remained unnamed until 2018.
Richard J. Butler and colleagues formally described it that year after studying rift fossils across Tanzania and Zambia.
It belongs to the unranked order Crurotarsi.
The animal is placed within the unranked family Paracrocodylomorpha.
Phylogenetic analysis classifies Mandasuchus as a loricatan that is more basal than Prestosuchus and distinct from, though closely related to, Ticinosuchus.
Mandasuchus lived during the Anisian stage of the Middle Triassic in Tanzania.
J. Michael Parrish debated whether Mandasuchus was a distinct genus, proposing it was synonymous with Ticinosuchus ferox based on similar postcranial bones until a formal description was published.
A 1965 study suggested Mandasuchus was a possible ancestor of prosauropods, though this hypothesis lacked explanation and is now considered highly improbable.
